name: Jiaogulan (Gynostemma pentaphyllum)
short: Case report: severe fall in platelets after 3+ months of jiaogulan, recovering after stopping. Report review: back pain with duloxetine. Trial review: fewer adverse events than lipid drugs.
text: A single case report describes a woman who had had a cerebral infarction (stroke) and developed severe thrombocytopenia, with a platelet count of 6.0 x 10^9/L and a white cell count of 3.27 x 10^9/L, after using Gynostemma pentaphyllum continuously for over three months; platelet counts rebounded to 156 x 10^9/L after it was stopped, and the authors concluded it may induce thrombocytopenia and that platelet levels should be closely monitored in long-term use. In a retrospective review of 1,816 adverse event reports, 30 reports judged to show a high probability of a causal relationship between an adaptogen-antidepressant interaction and the adverse event were included, and one of these was back pain with Gynostemma pentaphyllum and duloxetine; the authors wrote, about adaptogens in general, that pharmacokinetic interactions (inhibition of CYP enzymes and P-glycoprotein) with antidepressants may result in clinically significant adverse events. In contrast, a systematic review of 22 randomised trials with 2,407 people with dyslipidaemia, most of them at some or high risk of bias, found fewer adverse events with Gynostemma than with lipid-lowering drugs and concluded that use for more than 8 weeks appears safe. In a 12-week placebo-controlled trial of a heat-processed extract in 80 adults with obesity, no clinically significant changes in any safety parameter (adverse events, laboratory tests, electrocardiogram, vital signs) were observed; in a 16-week placebo-controlled trial of an extract taken by mouth in 117 overweight adults, the liver enzyme alanine aminotransferase differed significantly between groups at week 16, and the abstract does not say in which direction.
